title: The lamp of the body (Matthew 6:22–24)
hook: the eye is the lamp; you can't serve God and mammon

segments.voice: Yesterday, moths and rust, and your line was where your treasure is. Where did you put a little treasure, and did your heart follow? Day two hundred fifty-two, the end of the week.

Try working for two bosses at once. One wants the report by noon; the other wants you at a meeting at noon. One says cut costs; the other says spend. Sooner or later, you pick one, and the other one notices. Anyone who's had two jobs, or divorced parents with different rules, knows the feeling. Jesus has just said the heart follows the treasure. Now he pushes it further, with two pictures: a lamp, and a servant with two masters.
screen: `TWO BOSSES AT ONCE.` → `SOONER OR LATER, YOU PICK ONE.` → `A LAMP, AND TWO MASTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the lamp. In the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light." Single here translates a Greek word that means simple, undivided, and also generous. In Jewish idiom, a good eye meant a generous person, and an evil eye meant a stingy one. Proverbs says the one with a bountiful eye shall be blessed, for he gives his bread to the poor. So a single eye looks at the world openly and generously, and the whole person fills with light. A grasping eye darkens everything. Then the second picture, in the King James Bible: "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Serve here means serve as a slave. Not a part-time job. A slave can't belong fully to two owners. And mammon? It's an Aramaic word for wealth or property, the stuff you own and rely on. Some scholars think it comes from a root meaning that in which you trust, though nobody is sure. It wasn't the name of a god; medieval writers later turned Mammon into a demon, and the poet Milton put him in Paradise Lost. But Jesus uses it almost like a person, a rival master, because that's how money can act: it makes demands, it promises safety, it asks for your time and your worry. Look back at this week: the other cheek, love for enemies, giving in secret, few words, our Father, moths and rust, and now one master. Each asks: who, finally, do you belong to?
screen: `THE EYE IS THE LAMP.` · `SINGLE: UNDIVIDED, GENEROUS.` · `NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.` · `MAMMON: WEALTH YOU TRUST.` · then, large: `YE CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you look at most. Settle, and breathe. Think back over today. What did your eyes keep going to? Prices, feeds, other people's things, the clock, a face you love? Don't judge it. Just notice where your eye kept landing. Then picture your eye as a lamp: what would it look like to see today with a generous eye? If you pray, you can ask for a single eye. The bell holds the time.
Mammon. Aramaic for wealth, the things you own and trust; Jesus names it as a rival master. You can't serve both.
Your line: one master. Today, when money makes a demand on your worry, remind yourself who you belong to, and do one generous thing with a single eye. Day two hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Christians often speak of stewardship, holding money as something entrusted by God, and many practice regular giving, simple living or fasting from spending as ways to keep money a servant rather than a master.

notes: haplous ('single') as generous, and the good eye / evil eye idiom (Proverbs 22:9; Deuteronomy 15:9; Matthew 20:15): confirm.
Mammon etymology from 'mn ('that in which one trusts') is uncertain; phrased as 'some scholars think ... nobody is sure'.
Mammon as a demon in medieval writing (e.g. Peter Lombard, Aquinas) and in Milton's Paradise Lost Book 1: confirm.
Proverbs 22:9 is paraphrased close to KJV wording, not quoted.
